intro: Real work from inside S&P Global. Not the metrics, just how I actually got there.

stories.title: Betting on a shift nobody else was watching
stories.context: Compustat, S&P Global's flagship financial-data product
body: Compustat is one of S&P Global's oldest and most valuable data products. Its whole job is turning company filings into clean, comparable numbers, and for years that meant reading PDFs and HTML filings the hard way, with a mix of people and models trained to parse messy documents.

I noticed something nobody on the team was tracking closely: the world's filings were quietly moving to a machine-readable format. Companies were starting to file numbers that were already tagged and structured, not just typeset for a human to read. Most instincts in the industry right now are to point AI at every messy document and try to make extraction smarter. I thought that was solving the wrong problem for a growing share of our filings.

So I made the case for redesigning the pipeline around the filings that were already structured, and using a deterministic, rules-based engine to map them into our data model instead of a probabilistic one. In a business where being wrong about a number actually matters, explainable beats clever. It freed up real processing capacity, and it gave the team a foundation that gets more valuable every year, because more of the industry keeps moving toward structured filings, not away from them.
The lesson I keep coming back to: sometimes the biggest lever isn't a smarter model. It's noticing that the ground already shifted under a business everyone assumed hadn't changed.

stories.title: Finding the work two teams were quietly duplicating
stories.context: Fast Financials, S&P Global's real-time earnings product
body: Fast Financials exists because some customers pay a premium to get standardized earnings data within minutes of a company's release. A separate team processes the same company's fuller regulatory filings weeks later. On paper, these looked like two unrelated workflows serving two different documents.

When I actually mapped both processes end to end, I found something almost embarrassing: the core financial numbers, balance sheet, income statement, cash flow, were usually identical between the fast, early filing and the slower, later one. Two teams were quietly redoing the same expert judgment on the same numbers, just weeks apart, without ever comparing notes.

The insight wasn't technical, it was organizational. The first team's expert-validated work was trustworthy enough to reuse. So I designed a way for the second team to treat the earlier, human-checked data as a reference, and only ask a person to look again when the newly extracted numbers actually disagreed with it. Before asking anyone to trust this in production, I backtested the hypothesis against a large set of historical filings to make sure it held up.

What made this satisfying wasn't the automation. It was realizing a company can build the exact same expertise twice without anyone noticing, simply because two teams never sat down and compared what they were actually doing.

stories.title: Choosing restraint over a chatbot
body: A large internal support team was fielding the same handful of questions about our data platform over and over, phrased a hundred different ways. The obvious move, in an AI-everything moment, was to build a chatbot that could answer questions directly.

I didn't think that was the right problem to solve. When I actually read through the queries, most of them weren't new questions. They were old questions the team had already answered, sitting in a case history or a knowledge base article that nobody could easily find in the moment. This wasn't an answer-generation problem. It was a discovery problem wearing a support-ticket costume.

So instead of generating new answers, I built a product that surfaces the most relevant past resolutions and reference material for whatever an analyst is looking at, so they can find and reuse an answer that already exists rather than reconstruct it from scratch under time pressure. It meaningfully improved how quickly the hardest category of questions got resolved, and it gave analysts something they trusted more than a generated answer: an actual precedent, written by a colleague.
The bigger takeaway was about restraint. The flashy solution isn't always the right one. Sometimes the organization already has the answer, and the job is just to make it findable.

stories.title: The model isn't the moat
stories.context: AgentOps, the enterprise agent platform I currently lead
body: This is the project I'm leading right now, and the one I'm proudest of. S&P Global turns long, dense financial disclosures, sometimes hundreds of pages, into standardized, structured data. As AI agents got good enough to attempt this kind of work, the obvious instinct across the industry was to treat it as a prompting problem: write a good prompt, point it at a document, see what comes back.

That instinct doesn't hold up for serious, high-stakes work, and I wanted to prove why before we built anything on top of it. A prompt plus a two-hundred-page document is not a production system. The people who actually know how to do this correctly, our domain experts, have years of accumulated judgment written down as policy documents meant for a human reader, not a machine. An AI agent handed a raw policy document has no real idea what actually matters inside it.

So instead of chasing better prompts, I led the build of a platform that treats reliable AI as a systems problem, not a prompting problem. It converts expert policy into a structured, machine-usable format instead of leaving that translation to chance. It figures out which parts of a huge document actually matter using the organization's own history of where similar facts have shown up before, so an agent isn't reading blind. When multiple independent agents disagree with each other, that disagreement gets treated as a signal worth routing to a person, rather than being smoothed over by a single model's confidence score. And developers and domain experts share one place to see exactly where an agent went wrong and fix that specific piece, instead of guessing at the whole pipeline.

Two completely different teams used this same approach to build two different automations, each in about a month, which told us we'd actually built a reusable platform and not just one clever agent. My own role has shifted since then. I spend less time deepening any single use case now, and more time thinking about how to get more teams onto the same foundation, which turns out to be a different job than the one I started with.

If there's one belief this whole project is built on, it's that the model itself is not the moat. Everyone will eventually have access to roughly the same models. What's actually hard to copy is the system around the model: the context it's given, the way disagreement gets handled, the way failures get diagnosed and fixed by someone who understands the domain. That's the part that has to be deliberately built, and it's the part most people are still skipping.
